title: Hideyoshi Orders His Tea Master to Die
text:
Sen no Rikyu was the most influential tea master in sixteenth-century Japan. He shaped the wabi style of the tea ceremony: small rustic rooms, plain rough bowls, and an aesthetic of quiet simplicity. Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the warlord who unified Japan, made him his chief tea master and a trusted confidant. Hideyoshi also had a portable tea room covered in gold, the opposite of everything Rikyu's taste stood for.

In early 1591 Hideyoshi suddenly turned against him. One charge was that Rikyu had placed a wooden statue of himself in the upper story of the gate he had paid to restore at the Daitokuji temple in Kyoto, so that anyone entering, including Hideyoshi, passed beneath his feet. Another was that he had sold tea utensils at inflated prices. Hideyoshi exiled him to Sakai, then called him back to Kyoto and ordered him to commit seppuku. The statue was taken down and displayed at a place of execution.

Rikyu died in the spring of 1591, at about sixty-nine. Hideyoshi later is said to have regretted it, and Rikyu's descendants founded the tea schools that still exist today.
lesson: A leader who cannot tolerate an independent voice near him may destroy the very person whose judgment he most needed.
source: Contemporary diaries and letters; later Japanese histories of the tea ceremony
caveat: Hideyoshi's real reasons are unknown; historians propose political rivalry, aesthetic conflict and court intrigue.
